extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and educators interested in verbal humour theory and joke analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the General Theory of Verbal Humour (GTVH) to model, analyse, or compare individual instances of verbal humour by identifying and comparing the theory's Knowledge Resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script Opposition (SO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to the script opposition contained within Raskin’s Script-Based Semantic Theory of Humour and includes themes such as real (unreal), actual (non-actual), normal (abnormal), possible (impossible), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SO is the semantic contrast(s) exploited in the joke; authors point to comprehensive lists of semantic oppositions. Identifying the opposed scripts is central to explaining why a joke can be humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Mechanism (LM)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanism that connects the different scripts within a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LMs can range from a simple verbal technique like a pun to more complex logical mechanisms such as faulty logic or false analogies. Analyze how the LM links the opposed scripts to produce the humorous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation (SI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes activities, objects, instruments or props needed to tell the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SI captures the contextual and pragmatic elements that make the joke narrative work; identify the situational details that enable the script opposition and logical mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target (TA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies the person/people who become the ‘butt’ of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TA locates the social target(s) (e.g., ethnic groups, genders, professions). Consider how TA contributes to stereotype construction and the social effects of the humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Strategy (NS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers the narrative format of the joke, as either a simple narrative, a dialogue, or a riddle, and aims to classify different genres (and subgenres) of verbal humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NS is the macro-structural classification of the humorous text; Attardo expanded NS to include oral and printed humorous narratives of any length (not just short jokes), enabling categorization of one-liners through extended humorous literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (LA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consists of all the information necessary for the verbalization of a text; responsible for the exact wording and placement of the functional elements of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LA covers micro-level linguistic realization (lexical choices, word order, timing). Examine wording and phrasing as they realize the other KRs and the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical ordering and interaction of Knowledge Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Knowledge Resource, ordered hierarchically, can determine the parameters of the KRs below it and can be determined by the KRs above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed ordering implies top-down/bottom-up constraints when analyzing jokes; however, empirical tests (e.g., by Willibald Ruch) have had only partial success, so the ordering should be treated as a heuristic subject to empirical validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity metric via Knowledge Resource matching
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH can be used to model individual jokes and analyse the degree to which they are similar or different by identifying how many of the Knowledge Resources are identical for any two humorous pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, compare KRs across joke variants (e.g., light bulb joke variants that shift a single KR) and count matching KRs to quantify similarity; use this to cluster or contrast humorous texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability across verbal humorous texts (advantage over script-only theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because GTVH includes Narrative Strategy (NS), it can categorise any and all humorous texts, from spontaneous one-liners to funny stories and literature, whereas Raskin's earlier Script-Based Semantic Theory dealt only with jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use GTVH for a wide range of verbal humour analyses—short jokes, dialogues, extended narratives—while noting possible limits signalled by critiques (e.g., ordering issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and theoretical critiques of GTVH
rubrics_metrics.description: There have been discussions regarding the proposed ordering of the Knowledge Resources; empirical tests (e.g., Willibald Ruch) produced only partial support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying GTVH, be aware of critiques and that some claimed hierarchical relations may not be robust empirically; treat ordering as a research hypothesis rather than an immutable rule.
